name: Mali
summary_text: Mali's penal code announced in October 2024 and in force from 13 December 2024 criminalises same-sex conduct, an escalation under the military junta that reverses the previous position in which same-sex relations were not a criminal offence. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 6 November 2024, describes the penalties as harsh.  The statute also bans the undefined offence of "promoting" homosexuality and reaches any citizen seen to encourage it. Because the term is not defined in the code, the provision widens the range of people who can be charged well beyond those accused of conduct itself, and Human Rights Watch states that the drafting is broad enough for expansive application.  Before the code took effect, same-sex conduct was legal in Mali, but the vague "public indecency" provisions of Article 225 were already used against LGBT people and against gender-nonconforming expression. Presentation rather than conduct has historically been what draws police attention, so a trans visitor's visible gender expression, not only any intimacy, is the surface on which enforcement has previously operated.  The change arrived alongside a wider clampdown on opposition and media under the military junta, in a security environment marked by armed-group violence and instability. Societal stigma toward LGBT people was already assessed as significant by the United States State Department in its 2021 human rights report, before decriminalisation ended.  No entry, visa, or gender-marker documentation rules for trans travellers are documented in the sources available for this record.

name: Myanmar
summary_text: Consensual same-sex intimacy is a criminal offence in Myanmar under Section 377 of the Penal Code, a colonial-era provision reported as carrying life imprisonment or up to 10 years' imprisonment. Police apply it alongside vague public-decency provisions, and authorities have used it to detain people who cannot satisfactorily account for their presence. The provision remained in active use as recently as 2018, when the HIV-positive LGBTI advocate Aung Myo Htut was charged under it.  Since the coup of 1 February 2021 the risk environment has intensified. The National Unity Government recorded 17 LGBT people killed and two critically injured. Human Rights Myanmar's June 2024 submission to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial killings counted 5 to 12 killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas, identified intensified Section 377 enforcement as an aggravating factor in those deaths, and described militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws as endangering the right to life. Torture and sexual violence in detention are reported.  Transgender visitors face a separate layer of exposure. Myanmar does not permit transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth, so the state does not recognise their gender identity and no legal gender recognition procedure exists. Section 35(c) of the 1945 Police Act allows police to detain anyone they consider behaving suspiciously after sunset, criminalises face covering with up to three months' imprisonment, and is applied specifically against transgender people, who also report police harassment, sexual assault, mistreatment and extortion. A trans woman describing events in 2016 recounted arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night while police alleged sex work; in 2013 trans women in Mandalay were forced to strip and parade naked while photographed, an episode police called a public service.  There is no enforceable legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised: couples can cohabit and hold ceremonial marriages without legal action, but those ceremonies carry no legal standing.  Care access is constrained by the same regime. Section 377 was identified in 2013 as hampering the country's HIV response, and gay men, particularly those living with HIV or AIDS, face stigmatisation. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights names LGBTQ people as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law.
